decision_reason: A1 provides useful global activity structure, but walking and jogging differ mainly through intensity while frontal elevation of arms and waist bends forward share moderate intensity, cadence, smoothness, and high rotational motion. Splitting rotational motion by body segment adds a supported distinction for upper-limb, trunk, and lower-limb activity. Splitting translation into horizontal and vertical components improves transfer from climbing stairs to walking and jogging without relying on unsupported recording statistics.

attributes.name: motion_intensity
attributes.definition: Overall magnitude and energy of motion within a window, including both linear and rotational components.

attributes.name: cadence
attributes.definition: Rate at which a meaningful periodic motion unit repeats over time. Cadence measures repetitions per unit time, not the total number of repetitions in the recording.

levels.Low: No clear periodic repetition or a slow repetition rate.

attributes.name: smoothness
attributes.definition: Degree to which motion changes continuously rather than through sustained rapid fluctuations.

levels.Medium: Moderately smooth motion with some fluctuations.
levels.High: Continuous and smooth motion with little fluctuation.

attributes.name: impulsiveness
attributes.definition: Degree to which motion contains short, abrupt, high-magnitude changes or impacts.

levels.Low: Few or no pronounced abrupt peaks.

attributes.name: posture_inclination
attributes.definition: Average gravity-relative inclination of the global load-bearing body configuration within a window, rather than the orientation of an isolated moving limb.

levels.High: Strongly inclined or nearly horizontal relative to gravity.

attributes.name: posture_variability
attributes.definition: Extent to which the global load-bearing body configuration changes relative to gravity within a window, rather than local limb-orientation changes.

attributes.name: motion_regularity
attributes.definition: Temporal consistency and predictability of the motion pattern.

levels.Low: Irregular and poorly predictable motion pattern.
levels.Medium: Partly structured motion with moderate variability.

attributes.name: upper_limb_rotational_motion
attributes.definition: Prominence of angular or multiaxial motion primarily expressed by the instrumented upper limb.

levels.Low: Little or no upper-limb rotational motion.

attributes.name: trunk_rotational_motion
attributes.definition: Prominence of angular or multiaxial motion associated with movement of the trunk or torso.

levels.Low: Little or no trunk rotational motion.

attributes.name: lower_limb_rotational_motion
attributes.definition: Prominence of angular or multiaxial motion primarily expressed by the instrumented lower limb during leg-driven activity.

levels.Low: Little or no lower-limb rotational motion.

attributes.name: horizontal_translation
attributes.definition: Prominence of sustained translation along the approximately horizontal direction during locomotion.

levels.Low: Little or no sustained horizontal translation.
levels.High: Prominent sustained horizontal or forward locomotor translation.

attributes.name: vertical_translation
attributes.definition: Prominence of translation or velocity change along the approximately vertical direction during movement.

levels.Low: Little or no sustained vertical translation.
levels.High: Prominent sustained vertical translation or elevation.

operations.reason: Overall motion magnitude is supported by motion-energy capabilities and remains a useful ordinal contrast between standing or sitting, walking, jogging, and running.
Repetition rate is directly supported by periodicity capabilities and transfers from cycling and running to the walking and jogging distinction.
Rapid signal-change capabilities support this distinct temporal property, which complements intensity and cadence for locomotor activities.
Peak-change and impact-sensitive capabilities support a separate ordinal contrast for walking, jogging, running, and jumping.
Static gravity-relative orientation directly supports the distinction among upright, inclined, and horizontal global postures.
Gravity-angle variation supports global posture change and remains useful for separating static postures from bending and crouching.
Temporal recurrence and predictability are independently supported and provide a transferable distinction between structured cyclic motion and less predictable motion.

The original rotational dimension conflates movement from different instrumented body regions. Segment-specific angular and multiaxial structure is supported by the hand, chest, and ankle sensors and separates frontal arm elevation from trunk bending while also distinguishing leg-driven locomotion and cycling.

A single translation dimension hides the direction of locomotor progression. Translational proxies combined with gravity-relative orientation support a directional distinction between forward locomotion and elevation-oriented activity such as stair climbing.

semantic_redundancy_review: Motion_intensity, impulsiveness, and smoothness are related but measure magnitude, abrupt peaks, and continuity respectively. Cadence and motion_regularity both describe temporal structure, but cadence measures repetition rate while regularity measures predictability. Posture_inclination and posture_variability describe global gravity-relative configuration and its change, whereas the three segment-specific rotational attributes describe where angular or multiaxial motion is expressed. Horizontal_translation and vertical_translation are directional components of locomotor translation and are distinct from posture change because they describe movement through space rather than orientation alone. All final attributes are ordinal and are supported in principle by the listed orientation, rotational, motion-energy, jerk, periodicity, temporal-structure, gravity-variation, translational-proxy, and multiaxial-coupling capabilities.

_meta.validation: Semantic schema and complete A1-to-A2 lineage validated; no feature binding performed.
